content: The updated guidance for implementing the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) emphasizes a shift from the traditional model of facility designation as the primary outcome and driver of practice changes. For countries with a well-functioning national BFHI designation program that reaches most facilities providing maternity and newborn services, this guidance does not suggest discontinuing successful programs. Instead, these countries should develop a plan to integrate the revised Ten Steps into their national BFHI standards. A transition plan should outline when facilities are expected to comply with the updated standards and adopt the new tools. Facilities already designated or in the process of designation should be given adequate time to adjust their practices before the new standards become mandatory. Historically, many countries used Picasso’s artwork, Maternity, for plaques or posters to signify Baby-Friendly facilities. However, WHO and UNICEF will no longer provide reproductions of this image. Countries using designation as an incentive for BFHI compliance must create their own imagery. If mother-friendly criteria beyond the Ten Steps have been incorporated into designation standards, these can remain unless updates are necessary. While maintaining a designation program, countries should also work on integrating the Ten Steps into national policies, quality improvement initiatives, and maternal and child health programs. For countries without an active or successful BFHI program, the focus should be on integrating and institutionalizing the Ten Steps using a quality improvement approach at the facility level, supported by robust policies and accountability mechanisms. Priority actions to revitalize BFHI sustainably are outlined in the guidance. Staff and management at facilities previously designated as Baby-Friendly must be informed of policy changes, updated standards, and the necessary actions to comply with these standards. The revised Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding (2018) align with WHO’s 2017 guidelines and emphasize critical management procedures and clinical practices. These include having a written breastfeeding policy, training healthcare staff, informing pregnant women about breastfeeding benefits, supporting early initiation of breastfeeding, and ensuring rooming-in practices. Additional steps include promoting breastfeeding on demand, avoiding artificial teats or pacifiers, and fostering breastfeeding support groups for mothers upon discharge.
